title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself: your name, where you are from, where you live and which languages you speak.
intro: This unit gives you the personal pronouns and the verb 'to be' (છું, છે, છો…), which you will use in almost every sentence. You'll also meet the main question words, which in Gujarati sit just before the verb.

vocab.note: written/standard; in speech એ is more common
present: છું, છે, છીએ, છો; negative નથી
હું રહું છું, તમે રહો છો
dative subject: મને ગુજરાતી આવડે છે 'I know Gujarati'
after a word = 'also' (હું પણ); between clauses = 'but'

phrases.native: મને થોડું થોડું ગુજરાતી આવડે છે.
phrases.roman: mane thoḍuṃ thoḍuṃ gujarātī āvaḍe chhe.

grammar.title: Pronouns and the verb 'to be'
grammar.body:
The present tense of **હોવું** 'to be' changes with the subject:

હું **છું** *huṃ chhuṃ* — I am
તું **છે** *tuṃ chhe* — you are (intimate)
એ / તે **છે** *e / te chhe* — he/she/it is
અમે / આપણે **છીએ** *ame / āpaṇe chhīe* — we are
તમે / આપ **છો** *tame / āp chho* — you are (polite/plural)
એ લોકો / તેઓ **છે** *e loko / teo chhe* — they are

The negative is a single word for everyone: **નથી** *nathī* 'am not / is not / are not'. Note the two words for 'we': **અમે** excludes the listener, **આપણે** includes them ('you and I').

grammar.title: Question words go before the verb
grammar.body:
Question words — **શું** 'what', **કોણ** 'who', **ક્યાં** 'where', **ક્યાંથી** 'from where', **કેમ** 'why/how' — don't move to the front as in English. They sit where the answer would go, usually just before the verb.

For yes/no questions, keep the statement order and raise your voice at the end. You may put **શું** at the very beginning to mark a yes/no question, especially in writing.

grammar.title: 'I know Gujarati': મને … આવડે છે
grammar.body:
Gujarati often expresses knowing a skill with a **dative subject**: the person who knows is marked with -ને (મને 'to me', તમને 'to you'), and the language or skill is the grammatical subject of **આવડવું**. Literally: 'To me Gujarati comes'. You'll see more dative-subject verbs in Unit 5 (ગમવું 'to like').

મને *mane* 'to me', તને *tane* 'to you (intimate)', તમને *tamne* 'to you (polite)', એને *ene* 'to him/her'.

dialogue.title: A new classmate
dialogue.setting: Sam, a British student, meets Nirav at a Gujarati class in Vadodara.

lines.speaker: Nirav
lines.native: કેમ છો? તમારું નામ શું છે?
lines.roman: kem chho? tamāruṃ nām shuṃ chhe?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: મારું નામ સેમ છે. તમારું નામ?
lines.roman: māruṃ nām Sem chhe. tamāruṃ nām?
lines.en: My name is Sam. And yours?

lines.speaker: Nirav
lines.en: I'm Nirav. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: હું ઇંગ્લેન્ડથી છું, પણ અત્યારે વડોદરામાં રહું છું.
lines.roman: huṃ Iṅglenḍthī chhuṃ, paṇ atyāre Vaḍodarāmāṃ rahuṃ chhuṃ.
lines.en: I'm from England, but right now I live in Vadodara.

lines.speaker: Nirav
lines.native: બહુ સરસ! અમે બધા તમને મદદ કરીશું.
lines.roman: bahu saras! ame badhā tamne madad karīshuṃ.
lines.en: Very nice! We'll all help you.

culture: On meeting someone, Gujaratis quickly ask where you are from — and often which town or community your family comes from. Answering with a city (*Amdāvād*, *Surat*, *Rājkoṭ*) is perfectly fine. Gujarati speakers switch freely into English and Hindi words; don't be surprised if your Gujarati question gets a mixed answer.
